text: may occur. The disease is progressive, and median survival is poor. His- tologically, disease may be epithelioid, sarcomatoid, or a mixture of the two. The epithelioid type is the most common, and may be confused with adenocarcinoma (see non-small cell lung cancer, above). In patients with small epithelioid tumours, radical surgery may be con- sidered, but otherwise is seldom appropriate. Pleurode- sis is usually the treatment of choice in the management of pleural effusions associated with mesothelioma; pleurectomy is an alternative. Palliative radiotherapy may be effective for pain relief,1 but is generally of lim- ited value.2,3 Responses to single-agent chemotherapy have been in the region of 10 to 20%. Doxorubicin, epirubicin, mitomycin, cyclophosphamide, ifosfamide, cisplatin, and carboplatin have all been tried.1,4 Irinotecan, topotecan, gemcitabine, 670 Antineoplastics vinorelbine, docetaxel, and paclitaxel have also been in- vestigated.1,4 Combination chemotherapy, mostly with doxorubicin- or cisplatin-based regimens, have not shown any survival advantage over single-agent therapy.4 How- ever, encouraging results were obtained in a large phase 3 study using pemetrexed and cisplatin, and this combina- tion is generally considered to be standard first-line thera- py.1,2,4-6 The addition of raltitrexed to cisplatin has also im- proved response rates and overall survival,7 and some benefits have been seen with gemcitabine plus cisplatin,2,3 which has been suggested as second-line therapy.2,6 Other regimens, including vinorelbine compared with mitomy- cin, vinblastine, and cisplatin (MVP),5 and raltitrexed with oxaliplatin4 are being investigated.
